title: Thread-pool starvation
sub: The server doesn't crash, it crawls
cards/0/body:
ASP.NET Core has no context, so .Result won't hang. But every such request holds a pool thread while it waits for the database. Why it hurts so much comes down to how the pool grows:

  • up to the MinThreads threshold (by default, the number of cores) the pool creates threads immediately, on demand;
  • beyond the threshold it adds threads cautiously: roughly one every half second, until the queue clears. You can raise the threshold with ThreadPool.SetMinThreads.

Step by step: 8 cores, 100 requests with .Result arrive.

  • 1. 8 threads take 8 requests and block on .Result. The other 92 wait in the pool's queue.
  • 2. The database responses arrive. But the continuations that the blocked threads need go into the same queue, behind the new requests.
  • 3. There are no free threads: the blocked ones wait for their continuations, and the continuations wait for a free thread. The pool adds a thread every half second, and the new thread often picks up not a continuation but the next request, which blocks on .Result as well.
  • 4. Responses stretch to seconds while the CPU is almost idle.
cards/0/deep: In .NET 6+ the pool notices blocking on Task.Wait and .Result in its own threads and adds threads faster. That softens starvation but doesn't cure it.
cards/1/task: Add 16 requests with .Result and start the clock. How many threads are stuck, and how does the pool grow?
cards/2/task: Now the same 16 requests, but with await.
cards/3/q: 16 requests with .Result bloated the pool, while the same 16 requests with await were served by 4 threads. Why?
cards/3/options/0: With .Result a thread is stuck for the whole database wait; with await it's free while we wait and takes the next piece of work
cards/3/options/1: With await the database answers faster
cards/3/options/2: The pool knew in advance the requests were asynchronous and decided not to add threads
cards/3/explain: Waiting without a thread is the main benefit of async on a server. The pool doesn't need more threads because none of them is stuck.
cards/4/q: Under load, responses lag by seconds while the CPU is nearly idle. What do you suspect first?
cards/4/explain: An idle CPU with growing latency means the threads exist, but they're stuck.
cards/5/body: In dotnet-counters, watch the pool's queue length and its thread count. A growing queue and a thread count that creeps upward while CPU load stays low is a sure sign.
cards/5/deep: dotnet-counters monitor --counters System.Runtime shows ThreadPool Queue Length and ThreadPool Thread Count. In a process dump (dotnet-dump), starvation shows up as dozens or hundreds of threads whose stacks end in .Result or Wait.
cards/6/q: What can cause thread-pool starvation? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/0: .Result and .Wait() on tasks that query the database
cards/6/options/1: Thread.Sleep in code that runs on the pool
cards/6/options/2: A synchronous read from a slow disk in every request
cards/6/explain: Anything that holds a pool thread without doing work.
cards/7/q: A quick "fix": ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(500, 500). What do you say?
cards/7/options/0: It hides the symptom: the pool hands out many threads at once, but they still sit idle and eat memory; the cure is switching to await
cards/7/options/1: Great fix: blocking costs nothing anymore
cards/7/options/2: It will speed up the database
cards/7/explain: The MinThreads threshold removes the delay in growing the pool, not the blocking. Hundreds of waiting threads mean memory and context switches. The real cure is not to block.
